  • reover, in many cases he makes use, as far as possible, of their
  • guments to preliminarily build up and then refine his own position.
  • is way of carrying out the “duel” with the pramāṇa philosophers

  • stead of directly attacking his adversary, Utpaladeva seeks to exploit
  • e adversary’s intellectual ability to finally turn it back upon him.
  • e main technique on which Utpaladeva’s argumentation is based is the
  • e well known in śāstric debate as prasaṅga-viparyaya. The Buddhist
  • eas are not rejected at the outset but are rather apparently accepted

  • e main part of the Vivr̥ti passage edited here is devoted to the
  • scussion of the Buddhist concepts of “non-perception” (anupalabdhi)
  • d, less extensively, of “exclusion” (apoha) as the very core of
  • nceptual thought. If one accepts the self-contained nature of
  • gnition (as the Buddhist does), it becomes impossible to account for
  • ther of them. On seeing an empty surface we would not be allowed to
  • y that there is no jar there because the cognition of a certain object

  • gnitions later to be rejected. Yet the world of human knowledge,

  • scription of how an individual cognition works in isolation is
  • nsidered as basically correct, the capability of the individual

  • itary consciousness in which all of them are rooted, in a word: by the

  • th the topics of anupalabdhi and apoha will receive a separate and

  • d 1.6.1-5 for apoha). Here they are preliminarily discussed from a

  • are of itself as opposed to the cognition of the place together with a
  • r, is also aware of the place as “devoid of a jar”. In fact, if a jar

  • paladeva points out that we are dealing here with two distinct and
  • parate cognitions, which are bound to remain so: the one can by no

  • her arguments are taken into account in the text (see below). To

  • n by no means act as a common basis where two distinct cognitions may
  • et. No single cognition, Utpaladeva concludes, not even perceptual

  • th each other.
  • e starting point for the discussion of the apoha issue is clearly

  • ngth in the Svārthānumānapariccheda chapter of his Pramāṇa-Vārttika

  • ntinually threatened by erroneous superimpositions (samāropa), caused,

  • ct that in principle many superimpositions are possible; thus a

  • tter whether they derive from beginningless nescience or from other
